Program Structure
Why choose a PhD in Mathematics and Statistics?
Looking to turn your passion for mathematics and statistics into an impact at an advanced research level?
Our PhD program offers advanced study in two streams: Applied Mathematics or Applied Statistics, with distinct requirements for each stream, but a shared, collaborative community. In Applied Mathematics, major areas of specialization include dynamical systems, mathematical biology, numerical analysis, and operations research, while Applied Statistics focuses on developing and applying advanced statistical methods to complex real-world data.
The Department of Mathematics and Statistics is a highly active research environment, with faculty expertise spanning agent-based simulations, biostatistics, computational statistics, data science, machine learning, and infectious disease modelling.
Deep, focused research training
Work closely with expert supervisors in a vibrant department to complete an original PhD over 3-4 years.
Wide range of advanced research areas
Specialize in cutting-edge fields such as infectious disease modelling, scientific computing, quantum computing, machine learning, or statistical genetics.
Strong interdisciplinary and societal impact
Address real-world scientific and societal challenges through collaborations with industry, government, and interdisciplinary specializations

What you will learn – sample courses
The PhD degree is primarily a research degree. For that reason, coursework commonly comprises a smaller proportion of the student's effort than in the master's program. All courses are chosen in consultation with the student's advisory committee. That said, a sampling of coursework in the PhD program can include:
MATH*6011 - Dynamical Systems I
Study qualitative and quantitative behaviour of differential equations, including flows, bifurcations, and manifolds, with applications in biological, physical, and social systems.
MATH*6181 - Topics in Applied Mathematics I
Explore advanced, rotating topics in applied mathematics under faculty guidance through lectures, seminars, or project-based work.
STAT*6550 - Computational Statistics
Implement core computational methods in statistics such as Monte Carlo, MCMC, non-parametric techniques, and the EM algorithm.
STAT*6761 - Survival Analysis
Analyze time-to-event data using survival and hazard functions, censored data methods, and both parametric and semi-parametric models.
Program Information and Requirements
Admission Info and Application Instructions
For the Doctoral program, a recognized master’s degree obtained with high academic standing is required, minimum B (73 per cent) admission average. The Departmental Graduate Program Committee will consider applications for direct entry to PhD with an undergraduate degree in exceptional cases, and for transfer from M.Sc. to PhD. In any event, a member of the department's graduate faculty must agree to act as an advisor to the student.
Complete application submission instructions may also be found on the Office of Graduate Studies webpage or in the Graduate Calendar.
Application Deadlines and Entry Points
Entry point for the PhD in Math and Stats is Fall (September). The application deadline is July 31 (domestic) and February 28 (international). International applicants are encouraged to apply at least nine months in advance of their start date, and all applicants are advised to apply as early as possible due to supervisor availability.
Program Load/Study Options
The PhD in Mathematics and Statistics is typically completed in four years of full-time study or eight years of part-time study.
Tuition and Graduate Student Fees
The Office of Graduate and Postdoctoral studies provides estimated annual full-time tuition, fees, and living expenses for graduate students at the University of Guelph: Tuition, Fees and Cost of Living.
Funding your Graduate Studies
Full funding is typically provided for full-time, thesis-based students (who do not receive external funding) through a combination of scholarships, teaching assistantships, and/or research assistantships. For more information about funding your graduate studies at Guelph, please visit Funding Graduate Studies.
Collaborative Specializations
PhD students may enhance their studies by pursuing a collaborative specialization alongside their degree:
One Health: Available to students conducting thesis research with a One Health focus.
Learn more about collaborative specializations and eligibility in the Graduate Calendar.
Faculty Research Areas
The Department of Mathematics and Statistics is an active department with 23 faculty and over 50 graduate students. Specific research areas include:
Biomathematics, Differential Equations and Scientific Computing
Computational and Bayesian Statistics
Epidemiology, Biostatistics, and Bioinformatics
Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence
Mathematical and Statistical Pedagogy
Network Modelling and Spatial-Temporal Statistics
Operations Research
Statistical Finance and Probability
Quantum Information and Matrix Analysis
Learn more about collaborative specializations and eligibility in the Graduate Calendar.
